analysis.one_liner: Doubles the research tax credit rate for businesses and expands startup access to the credit.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in June 2022 and received no hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would double the main federal research tax credit from 20% to 40% of qualifying research spending, double the alternative simplified version from 14% to 28%, and make the credit more generous for companies with little prior research activity. It would also let qualifying small startups claim up to $500,000 of the credit against their payroll taxes, up from $250,000, and loosen the revenue limit for eligibility. The bill never moved after being referred to the tax-writing committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that spend heavily on research and development — typically large technology, pharmaceutical, aerospace, and manufacturing firms — would pay less in federal tax on the same research activity. Small startups with revenue under the eligibility threshold would gain the ability to offset up to $500,000 of payroll tax with the credit, which matters most to early-stage companies with no income tax bill to offset.

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the regular research credit rate from 20% to 40% of qualifying research expenses and the alternative simplified credit from 14% to 28%. [S3] [S2]

Doubles the amount of the credit certain small businesses can apply against payroll tax liabilities, from $250,000 to $500,000, and ties the gross-receipts eligibility threshold to the inflation-adjusted section 448(c)(1) dollar amount instead of a fixed $5 million. [S3]
Raises the credit rate available to taxpayers that had no research expenses in the preceding three years, from 6% to half the standard rate. [S3] [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through the revenue the government gives up when research credits cut corporate tax bills. Since the expanded credits have no offset in the bill, the cost would add to deficits unless Congress cut spending or raised other taxes to cover it. Companies that already benefit from the credit would gain the most, because the rate doubles on research spending they were doing anyway.

drawbacks.text: Doubling the credit rate doubles the revenue cost for every firm already claiming it, including large profitable corporations, without any condition that the extra money produce research that would not have happened anyway. [S3]
The bill includes no pay-for: the forgone revenue would add to federal deficits and be borne by taxpayers at large. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The startup payroll-tax provision has a defensible aim: early-stage companies with no tax bill can lose the value of the credit entirely, and raising the cap targets help toward them. But the headline of the bill is doubling a credit whose main claimants are large, profitable R&D-intensive firms, and the bill pays for none of it. Weighing a broad corporate tax cut with an unoffset deficit cost against the uncertain spillover benefit of more research spending, the costs fall more clearly on the public than the benefits do.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2022 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which took no action on it before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Jackie Walorski (R-IN) introduced the bill on June 28, 2022, joined by Rep. Jodey Arrington as an original cosponsor. [S3]
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day. [S5] [S1]
Seven House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did. [S4]
The bill's only actions were introduction and referral; it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers at large are better off on paper because the unoffset corporate tax cut never became law. The 20% and 14% research credit rates remain in place rather than doubling to 40% and 28%. R&D-intensive companies lost the chance to cut their tax bills, and startups lost the higher payroll-tax offset.

industries.note: Doubling the credit rate from 20% to 40% (and 14% to 28% for the simplified credit) would cut federal tax bills for firms already claiming the credit on research they were doing anyway, with no offset for the lost revenue. Ordinary taxpayers bear the cost through deficits or offsetting taxes, while any benefit to the public from additional innovation is indirect and uncertain.

Startups with no income tax liability would be able to offset up to $500,000 of payroll taxes with the credit, up from $250,000, and a looser revenue threshold would make more of them eligible. This targets real help at companies that would otherwise get little value from a research credit.
